sources.title: Preparing Your Child for a New Sibling
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts)
sources.quote: It's common for them to feel jealousy toward the newborn and to act out. ... Encourage older kids to talk about their feelings about the new baby. If a child cannot express those feelings, don't be surprised if they test limits or revert to speaking in baby talk. If your child acts up, don't bend the rules, but understand what feelings may be motivating that behavior. It could be a sign that your child needs more one-on-one time with you, but make it clear that although his or her feelings are important, they have to be expressed in appropriate ways. ... Take advantage of chances for one-on-one time with older kids. Spend time together while the baby is sleeping and, if possible, set aside time each day for older kids to get one parent's undivided attention. ... If your child shows more interest in the baby, you can encourage that by ... reading books about childbirth (make sure they're age-appropriate) ... Include them as much as possible in the daily activities involving the baby so that they don't feel left out. ... If your child expresses no interest in the baby, don't be alarmed and don't force it. It can take time. ... Continue to send your older child to childcare or to school, if you're able. ... keeping normal routines is helpful for siblings. ... Also remind relatives and friends that your older child might want to talk about something other than the new baby.
sources.supports: Jealousy toward a newborn is common; talk about feelings; acting out and baby talk can follow; keep the rules and understand the feeling behind them; daily one-on-one time (for example while the baby sleeps); include the older child in the baby's daily care without forcing interest; books about the new baby are one way to encourage interest; keep routines such as childcare; relatives can ask about the older child too. Applied to Israeli families as general child-health advice.

sources.title: Sibling Relationships: How to Help Your Kids Build Healthy Bonds
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (adapted from Healthy Children Magazine; last updated 4/6/2026)
sources.quote: While time together as a family is important, one-on-one time with each child is important too. Try fitting it into your daily routines, such as during a nightly chat at bedtime ... These are times for you to truly tune in to them and for your child to know they have your full attention.
sources.supports: Short one-on-one time with each child, for example a chat at bedtime, so the child knows they have your full attention.

sources.title: Sibling Rivalry
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Jennifer Shroff Pendley, PhD, reviewed March 2023)
sources.quote: Most brothers and sisters have some degree of jealousy or competition, which can lead to arguments and bickering. ... Give your kids one-on-one attention directed to their interests and needs. ... Show and tell your kids that, for you, love is not something that comes with limits. Let them know that they are safe, important, and loved, and that their needs will be met.
sources.supports: Some jealousy between siblings is common; one-on-one attention directed to each child's interests; telling the child that love has no limits and that they are safe, important and loved.

sources.title: Preparing Your Child for a New Sibling
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts)
sources.quote: It's common for them to feel jealousy toward the newborn and to act out. ... Encourage older kids to talk about their feelings about the new baby. If a child cannot express those feelings, don't be surprised if they test limits or revert to speaking in baby talk. If your child acts up, don't bend the rules, but understand what feelings may be motivating that behavior. It could be a sign that your child needs more one-on-one time with you, but make it clear that although his or her feelings are important, they have to be expressed in appropriate ways. ... Take advantage of chances for one-on-one time with older kids. Spend time together while the baby is sleeping and, if possible, set aside time each day for older kids to get one parent's undivided attention. ... If your child shows more interest in the baby, you can encourage that by ... reading books about childbirth (make sure they're age-appropriate) ... Include them as much as possible in the daily activities involving the baby so that they don't feel left out. ... If your child expresses no interest in the baby, don't be alarmed and don't force it. It can take time. ... Continue to send your older child to childcare or to school, if you're able. ... keeping normal routines is helpful for siblings. ... Also remind relatives and friends that your older child might want to talk about something other than the new baby.
sources.supports: Jealousy toward a newborn is common; talk about feelings; acting out and baby talk can follow; keep the rules and understand the feeling behind them; daily one-on-one time (for example while the baby sleeps); include the older child in the baby's daily care without forcing interest; books about the new baby are one way to encourage interest; keep routines such as childcare; relatives can ask about the older child too. Applied to Israeli families as general child-health advice.

sources.title: Sibling Rivalry
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Jennifer Shroff Pendley, PhD, reviewed March 2023)
sources.quote: Most brothers and sisters have some degree of jealousy or competition, which can lead to arguments and bickering. ... Give your kids one-on-one attention directed to their interests and needs. ... Show and tell your kids that, for you, love is not something that comes with limits. Let them know that they are safe, important, and loved, and that their needs will be met.
sources.supports: Some jealousy between siblings is common; one-on-one attention directed to each child's interests; telling the child that love has no limits and that they are safe, important and loved.

sources.title: Sibling Relationships: How to Help Your Kids Build Healthy Bonds
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (adapted from Healthy Children Magazine; last updated 4/6/2026)
sources.quote: While time together as a family is important, one-on-one time with each child is important too. Try fitting it into your daily routines, such as during a nightly chat at bedtime ... These are times for you to truly tune in to them and for your child to know they have your full attention.
sources.supports: Short one-on-one time with each child, for example a chat at bedtime, so the child knows they have your full attention.

sources.title: Preparing Your Child for a New Sibling
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts)
sources.quote: It's common for them to feel jealousy toward the newborn and to act out. ... Encourage older kids to talk about their feelings about the new baby. If a child cannot express those feelings, don't be surprised if they test limits or revert to speaking in baby talk. If your child acts up, don't bend the rules, but understand what feelings may be motivating that behavior. It could be a sign that your child needs more one-on-one time with you, but make it clear that although his or her feelings are important, they have to be expressed in appropriate ways. ... Take advantage of chances for one-on-one time with older kids. Spend time together while the baby is sleeping and, if possible, set aside time each day for older kids to get one parent's undivided attention. ... If your child shows more interest in the baby, you can encourage that by ... reading books about childbirth (make sure they're age-appropriate) ... Include them as much as possible in the daily activities involving the baby so that they don't feel left out. ... If your child expresses no interest in the baby, don't be alarmed and don't force it. It can take time. ... Continue to send your older child to childcare or to school, if you're able. ... keeping normal routines is helpful for siblings. ... Also remind relatives and friends that your older child might want to talk about something other than the new baby.
sources.supports: Jealousy toward a newborn is common; talk about feelings; acting out and baby talk can follow; keep the rules and understand the feeling behind them; daily one-on-one time (for example while the baby sleeps); include the older child in the baby's daily care without forcing interest; books about the new baby are one way to encourage interest; keep routines such as childcare; relatives can ask about the older child too. Applied to Israeli families as general child-health advice.

sources.title: Developmental Milestones: 12 Months (1 Year)
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Larissa Hirsch, MD, reviewed June 2025)
sources.quote: Your 1-year-old toddler is a unique person who grows and learns at their own pace. They may be more talkative or less talkative than their peers, so try not to compare. Your toddler may: say one or two words plus "mama" and "dada" ... recognize and understand many words, even if they can't say them ... make gestures, like pointing at a toy ... Skip the "baby talk" and use the correct words for people, places, and things. Speak slowly and clearly — your toddler is listening. ... respond to your child's gestures by naming the item or person they gesture to, like "Yes, that is a cat." ... sing and play rhyming games ... read colorful picture books ... Share your concerns — even little ones — with your child's doctor.
sources.supports: Toddlers understand many words before they say them; pointing is a gesture to answer by naming the item; use the correct words instead of baby talk and speak slowly; songs, rhymes and picture books; children differ in how talkative they are; ask the doctor about concerns.

sources.title: First words and little sentences: 1 to 2 years
sources.quote: Everyday moments like cooking, playing and having fun help your child to learn new words, put sentences together, and practise having conversations. ... Chatting about your daily routine, like getting dressed, is a great way for your child to hear the same words every day. This helps them to start matching words they hear to things and actions. ... Name objects and offer your child choices, for example, "Do you want an apple or an orange?". ... Look at picture books together – give your child time to point things out and talk about what they can see ... Singing songs and rhymes is a fun way to introduce your child to new words and sounds ... Make sure to look at your little one so they can see your expressions. ... Follow your child's lead ... Avoid screen time for your baby or toddler. ... Remember, children learn to talk at different ages. If you are worried, speak to your health visitor or nursery key worker

sources.title: Developmental Milestones: 12 Months (1 Year)
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Larissa Hirsch, MD, reviewed June 2025)
sources.quote: Your 1-year-old toddler is a unique person who grows and learns at their own pace. They may be more talkative or less talkative than their peers, so try not to compare. Your toddler may: say one or two words plus "mama" and "dada" ... recognize and understand many words, even if they can't say them ... make gestures, like pointing at a toy ... Skip the "baby talk" and use the correct words for people, places, and things. Speak slowly and clearly — your toddler is listening. ... respond to your child's gestures by naming the item or person they gesture to, like "Yes, that is a cat." ... sing and play rhyming games ... read colorful picture books ... Share your concerns — even little ones — with your child's doctor.
sources.supports: Toddlers understand many words before they say them; pointing is a gesture to answer by naming the item; use the correct words instead of baby talk and speak slowly; songs, rhymes and picture books; children differ in how talkative they are; ask the doctor about concerns.

sources.title: First words and little sentences: 1 to 2 years
sources.quote: Everyday moments like cooking, playing and having fun help your child to learn new words, put sentences together, and practise having conversations. ... Chatting about your daily routine, like getting dressed, is a great way for your child to hear the same words every day. This helps them to start matching words they hear to things and actions. ... Name objects and offer your child choices, for example, "Do you want an apple or an orange?". ... Look at picture books together – give your child time to point things out and talk about what they can see ... Singing songs and rhymes is a fun way to introduce your child to new words and sounds ... Make sure to look at your little one so they can see your expressions. ... Follow your child's lead ... Avoid screen time for your baby or toddler. ... Remember, children learn to talk at different ages. If you are worried, speak to your health visitor or nursery key worker

sources.title: Developmental Milestones: 12 Months (1 Year)
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Larissa Hirsch, MD, reviewed June 2025)
sources.quote: Your 1-year-old toddler is a unique person who grows and learns at their own pace. They may be more talkative or less talkative than their peers, so try not to compare. Your toddler may: say one or two words plus "mama" and "dada" ... recognize and understand many words, even if they can't say them ... make gestures, like pointing at a toy ... Skip the "baby talk" and use the correct words for people, places, and things. Speak slowly and clearly — your toddler is listening. ... respond to your child's gestures by naming the item or person they gesture to, like "Yes, that is a cat." ... sing and play rhyming games ... read colorful picture books ... Share your concerns — even little ones — with your child's doctor.
sources.supports: Toddlers understand many words before they say them; pointing is a gesture to answer by naming the item; use the correct words instead of baby talk and speak slowly; songs, rhymes and picture books; children differ in how talkative they are; ask the doctor about concerns.

sources.title: First words and little sentences: 1 to 2 years
sources.quote: Everyday moments like cooking, playing and having fun help your child to learn new words, put sentences together, and practise having conversations. ... Chatting about your daily routine, like getting dressed, is a great way for your child to hear the same words every day. This helps them to start matching words they hear to things and actions. ... Name objects and offer your child choices, for example, "Do you want an apple or an orange?". ... Look at picture books together – give your child time to point things out and talk about what they can see ... Singing songs and rhymes is a fun way to introduce your child to new words and sounds ... Make sure to look at your little one so they can see your expressions. ... Follow your child's lead ... Avoid screen time for your baby or toddler. ... Remember, children learn to talk at different ages. If you are worried, speak to your health visitor or nursery key worker
sources.supports: Talk through daily routines so the child hears the same words every day; name objects and offer choices; picture books with time to point; songs and rhymes; follow the child's lead; avoid screens under 2; children learn to talk at different ages and a health professional can be asked. A UK page, applied to Israeli families as general advice.
